q: When do a precursor's electricity emissions count in a CBAM figure?
title: CBAM precursor electricity emissions rule
short: It depends on the finished good. If the good is in Annex II (steel, aluminium, hydrogen), a precursor outside Annex II still brings its indirect emissions. If the good is outside Annex II (cement, fertilisers), a precursor that is in Annex II, such as hydrogen, does not bring its indirect emissions.
audience: Indian steel, fertiliser and ammonia producers

p: Annex II of the CBAM Regulation lists goods for which only direct emissions count: aluminium, hydrogen, electricity, and iron and steel.

sections.h: Case 1: finished good in Annex II
p: If its production uses a precursor not listed in Annex II, that precursor's indirect emissions are still included. Example from the guidance: agglomerated iron ore (CN 26011200) feeding pig iron. Iron ore is in Annex I but not Annex II, so its indirect emissions travel up the chain.

sections.h: Case 2: finished good not in Annex II
p: If its production uses a precursor that is listed in Annex II, the precursor's indirect emissions are left out. Example: hydrogen made separately, for instance by electrolysis on the ammonia site, then used to make ammonia.
In a generic Haber-Bosch plant, hydrogen is only an intermediate step and its indirect emissions cannot be separated. Then the indirect emissions of the whole process are included.
Ammonia and fertilisers carry electricity emissions; steel does not, except through precursors such as ore. Check which case you are in before asking suppliers for electricity data.

senseible: Senseible reads electricity bills and purchase invoices into dated records. Which precursor rule applies to your goods depends on the CN codes, which you or your verifier confirm.
